questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I wanted to go to an English-speaking country, and I've never been in the United States, so it seemed like the obvious destination. US culture has a big impact and is generally the leader in many aspects of our world. Additionally, as an economics student US economy is interesting since it's the biggest economy in the world. 
Lastly, I wanted to go to a state/city where I could get the real college experience and be close to some of the “must see” cities since I wanted to travel. NC State/Raleigh is indeed such place.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was unbelievable! NC State's facilities are very good. The university literally offers everything in terms of clubs, trips etc. The weather is very good. The southern hospitably is indeed a thing and something you must experience. It's impossible to list everything but the experience overall contained everything. Travelling, new friends, day trips, frat parties, sports games (football, soccer, basketball, volleyball, wrestling etc.) and much more. And of course, classes! My classes were interesting, but the academic level isn't a high as back at University of Copenhagen.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. The university is very good a sending e-mail's upon arrival and making check-list for you. They are also good at answering questions through e-mail's if you have any. There is generally a lot of information on NC State's website in terms of what to do upon arrival.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Because of Covid-19 we had online intro days where they welcomed all the students and assisted with what to do. This was very useful even though it probably would be better if it was physical and under normal circumstances.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The assistance and orientation upon arrival was very good and easy to understand and follow. The orientation after I arrived was good given the circumstance. But not matter what, an online format is just not as good. But NC State did a good job and that's why I give it 5/5.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Different residence halls. You can apply through their online portal which is quite easy and straight forward. I was a part of the Global Village and lived in Alexander Hall. Here international students are paired with American roommates.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
Lots of meal plan options. I didn't choose one because (1) there was a kitchen at Alexander Hall, (2) the meal plans are expensive in my opinion and (3) I preferred to try the different food in the Raleigh area and (4) it's not a burden for me to cook. You can always try a meal plan the first two weeks and then change or cancel it if it's not something for you. I didn't choose one before I arrived and found out quickly that it wasn't something for me.
The kitchen at Alexander is good and covered my needs. However, there wasn't any kitchen equipment's so you couldn't do the fanciest dishes unless you bought it all you self.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Housing on campus is mandatory for first-year students which means fewer rooms for exchange students. However, it seemed like housing off campus was easy to get. Also, when it says “off campus” which includes (Stanhope, Valentine Commons, University Towers etc.) it is still very close to the campus. 
Alexander Hall properly has the best location. It's on central campus and close to the Wellness and Recreation Center (best gym I've ever seen), Talley Student Union etc. 
When it comes to Global Village, I think Alexander Hall was better before. It seems like that because of the first-year on campus living recruitment lot of the Americans at Alexander Hall didn't actively apply for the Global Village so I expected more especially after reading previous students experience at Alexander Hall. Because of Covid-19 we also had to wear a mask in the residence hall all the time. This was a bit annoying because you didn't feel home when you had to wear a mask. This was the case for all the facilities at campus, so you got used to it. 
However, the exchange students at Alexander Hall had a good time and I met some nice Americans, and the location was very convenient. So overall, I would recommend Alexander Hall and Global Village.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you want to be a part of the Global Village and live in Alexander Hall, make a good application! Other exchange students I talked with also applied but didn't get a room. However, bear in mind that the Americans (your potential roommate) is probably very young (18-21 years old). My roommate was 18 and I am 26 (when I applied, I thought the Americans were older based on previous study abroad evalutions)! I was very much in doubt but gave it a try (you can cancel your room or get another roommate within the first two weeks). He ended up being very cool and mature and we had a good time. He also ended up spending time with other the exchange students and was awesome!

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was very easy. They give you all the necessary information.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You basically find the courses you want in the course catalogue and then you make a prioritized list. You then later find out whether you got a spot in the class.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can e-mail and ask all the questions you may have. You can also e-mail the professor/instructor if you have any course specific questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes that I registered for. If you don't, then don't worry. The first two weeks or so you can add and drop classes (very normal in US). If the class you want is full, you can always talk to the professor, and they will most likely give you a spot (what I heard from other exchange students). The most important part is that you can get preapproval (“forhåndsgodkendelse”) for the classes you attend abroad.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to get preapproval from UCPH. Don't worry too much if you don't get a class. Everybody is basically adding and dropping classes the first weeks so you will find out when you arrive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The classes I had was overall interesting and different than what I'm used to from UCPH in terms of teaching style and examination. The academic level was lower at NC State which made the workload lower than back at UCPH.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I'm a master student at UCPH but took only BA courses at NC State. This obviously made the workload and academic level lower since the graduate courses are more specialized and thus the workload is bigger. However, this suited me fine since my choice of going on exchange was more about speaking English, experiencing another culture, traveling etc. This was for me more important than the academics.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching style at NC State is more like gymnasium in Denmark. The classes are small, more interaction between the professor and students, more exams, homework and more. I liked that because the teaching style at UCPH can sometimes be monotonous since there is not a lot of interaction and the economics exams at UCPH are (mostly) one shot. In US you have midterms, homework, and final exams. This make it less stressful, and the workload is spread out through the whole semester.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
I was enrolled in:

EC 431 Labor Economics
EC 449 International Finance
ARE 336 Introduction to Resource and Environmental Economics 
BUS 320 Financial Management

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend EC 431 Labor Economics. Professor Melinda Morrill is very good and engaged. She makes sure to interact with the students and was very welcoming. The class was also very interesting and is a huge field within economics.
The course EC 449 International Finance was also interesting and specially to have an American view on the world economy. The teacher was good at explaining and had a clear structure.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I didn't have any unexpected costs but there are costs when getting your VISA that I didn't expect. But overall, the costs, that I had, was expected. Because of Covid-19 local transportation in Raleigh was free.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Communication is expensive in US. I would recommend Mint Mobile. You can get 3 months for 45 dollars, and you get 4 GB data + unlimited talk and text. That's the cheapest option that I knew of, and I would say that it was enough for my needs since you can get Wi-Fi most places if you need more data. Vegetables are expensive compared to Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very much! The options are endless, and you can easily find a club, sports etc. within your interests.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The gym offers a lot of different classes. And offers day trips and activities that you can sign up to.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend the yoga classes. The instructors were very good, and you just signed up through their app. 
Go bouldering in the gym. You can rent shoes in the gym.
I would also recommend the social activities through the gym. I standup paddled and went to the day trip at Stone Mountain. This was a good way to meet other Americans and see some of the beautiful nature in US.
In general – use the facilities in the gym. You can go swimming, spinning, sauna, table tennis, squash, weightlifting and much more. You can rent almost anything you need through the gym – rackets, towels, t-shirts, basketball, football etc.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go see the big cities on the east coast - New York City, Boston, Philadelphia, Washington DC, and Miami. Raleigh has a good airport and train station. Rent a car and go for a road trip with other exchange students. Museums are free in Raleigh - go see them. Run the City of Oaks Marathon. Reedy Creek Trail is very good for a run/walk. Go see Carolina Hurricanes. Go see Durham Bulls. Go downtown and have a beer or two. Go to a pub and see real football (Americans somehow call it soccer).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. US is not that different to Denmark. Americans are also very hospital, so you quickly feel welcome. Just be openminded and then you will adjust to the local culture quickly.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Staying at Alexander Hall made it easier for me since I socialized with my roommate and his brother a lot. But joining an intramural team and/or club will make it easier. Again, Americans are easy to talk with once you open and basically just talk.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not anything particularly. Everything is bigger!

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Hospitality! Believe me. Once you been North and then go back to the South you will understand. In the South it's rude to not hold the door for someone. And once you get used to it you will also start finding it very rude when other people don't do it.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1.	It will be the time of your life! It will go fast so enjoy it as much as possible. You will be nervous and excited which is a part of it. But once you get there and everything is sorted out you will have a very good time. Don't be too serious about the academics. 
2.	Be openminded and just talk. That's the way to socialize, meet other people, and become better at English. 
3.	Make sure to talk and socialize with locals. It can be very easy to just hang out and talk with exchange students. But try to talk and socialize with Americans as well.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember to bring an adapter and an extension cord. Flip flops for the shower. Googles for swimming. Backpack for weekend trips. Get your insurance from Denmark (much cheaper than the one the university offers). Be patient with all the paperwork – it's worth it in the end!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Becoming more comfortable speaking English and experiencing another culture. You expand your horizon and experience an unbelievable country in terms of the nature, people, history, and culture.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: For me it was being away from my girlfriend during the whole stay (because of Covid-19 she couldn't come visit me) and family and friends.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Just do it! You may have questions, doubts and so on but once you go you will have the time of your life. I can highly recommend NC State. Very welcoming atmosphere, real college experience, unbelievable physical and educational facilities, Southern state, good weather, close to beautiful nature, close to mayor cities and much more. Go WolfPack!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
